title: Hard 12: the 3/4 boundary
subtitle: 2 introductions · 5 practice · 5 independent tasks
theory: Hard 12 totals 12 with no ace counted as 11. For our 6D, S17, DAS, late surrender, peek, 3:2 profile, stand against 4–6; hit against 2–3 and 7–A. Do not group all small dealer cards together: 3 and 4 sit on opposite sides of the boundary. For example, 10+2 against 4 is Stand, but against 3 is Hit. This is a choice with a better average result, not a guaranteed win. A pair of sixes belongs to a separate Split lesson and is excluded here. Try two unscored examples, then ten tasks. Correcting a mistake does not replace your first answer.

scenarios.explanation: Hard 12 against 4–6: Stand. Another card adds bust risk; here letting the dealer finish their hand is the better choice.
scenarios.contrast: Compare: 9+3 against 3 → Hit; the same hand against 4 → Stand. Only the dealer upcard changes.

title: Soft 18: check Double
subtitle: 2 introductions · 5 practice · 5 independent tasks
theory: Soft 18 contains an ace currently counted as 11. For 6D, S17, DAS, late surrender, peek, 3:2: double against 3–6, stand against 2/7/8, hit against 9/10/A. If Double is unavailable against 3–6, stand rather than hit. For example, A+7 against 6 is Double, but A+2+5 against 6 is Stand: the hand is still soft, but doubling is unavailable after a third card. Against 9, soft 18 is not an automatic stand. Start with two unscored examples, then ten tasks. Your first answer matters, not a random monetary outcome.

scenarios.explanation: Soft 18 against 3–6 on the first two cards: Double. The ace gives flexibility and the weak dealer upcard makes doubling preferable.
scenarios.contrast: Compare: A+7 against 6 → Double; A+2+5 against 6 → Stand; A+7 against 9 → Hit. Every hand is soft 18.

title: Hi-Lo: cancel pairs
subtitle: One card at a time · preserve the starting RC
theory: In Hi-Lo, 2–6 contribute +1, 7–9 contribute 0, and 10/J/Q/K/A contribute −1. A low and a high card cancel: 3+K change the count by zero. A neutral 8 changes nothing. Each card can belong to only one pair: 5,K,2 leave +1, not zero. Cancellation preserves the starting RC rather than resetting it: at RC −2, the pair 3,K leaves −2. Reveal cards with the button, keep count mentally, then enter the final RC with −/+ controls. Tags are visible in two introductory examples, then hidden until a hint or feedback. The final five tasks have no hints. This is a local simulation, not input from an external table.

scenarios.explanation: Starting RC 0. Card tags: 3: +1, K: -1. Final RC 0. Add the values left after cancelling low and high cards.
scenarios.contrast: Compare: 5,K change RC by 0, but 5,K,2 change it by +1. The king is already used in the first pair. Starting at RC +2, the final counts would be +2 and +3.

mistakes.count: Your RC differs. Check the starting count, the ace (−1), neutral 7–9, and whether any card was cancelled twice.
